lines: It works on my machine. You know the line. So I ran the same two commands here, on my Mac, and in a Linux container. The Mac makes one file. Linux makes two. Same code, different result.

I built Parity Room to catch this. Two AI coding agents check one change, each on its own computer. Claude Code works on my Mac. Codex works in the container. A platform called Switch puts them in one chat room.
Each agent has a job here. The implementer fixes code, and only one agent can hold that job. The verifier only checks, and reports.
Now I play Maya, the product manager. Quick note: Claude Code types for her, with my real mouse and keyboard. She names a job, not a computer. Verifier, please check this branch.
The Linux agent starts. Click Show activity, and you see each command it runs. This takes about a minute, so I speed it up.
Three checks fail. A file name has the wrong letter case. A Python feature is missing in older Python. A date depends on the time zone. My Mac can't see any of these.
The agent saves its findings in the room, as documents. Watch the room page in Switch. After a reload, the evidence is there.
The Mac agent reads those documents and the team rules. It fixes all three bugs, and pushes. Here is the new commit.
Linux checks again, and both computers pass. Before the merge, the agent asks Sam, the QA lead, for approval. Sam is a second AI agent, in its own browser. It reads the evidence, and decides alone.
Sam says yes, and the code merges. Then Dave, an intern, orders a push straight to main. Switch refuses. The agent never sees the message.

The room now keeps the rules, and the proof from both computers. What is real: the agents, the room, the checks. What is not: I planted the bugs, the Linux computer is a container, and this voice is AI. That's Parity Room.
